title: One street, many directions cards
allegory: A tensor is one long street of numbered houses plus a directions card; the card (the stride) says how many doors to walk per step along each axis, so a new card gives a new shape without moving a single house.
map: one long street of 20 numbered houses
the flat storage buffer behind a (4, 5) tensor
the directions card: 5 doors per row, 1 door per column
the house where your route starts
writing a new card while every house stays put
transpose, reshape and slicing: new size and stride over the same memory
a card that says walk 0 doors: stay at the same house
stride 0: broadcasting and expand repeat an element for free

cap.1: You see 4 rows of 5 numbers. The computer sees one long street of 20 houses, numbered 0 to 19. So which house is row 2, column 3?
cap.2: A (4, 5) tensor looks 2-D, but its storage is one flat buffer of 20 numbers. Something has to turn the index [2, 3] into a position in that buffer.
cap.3: A tensor is a view over flat 1-D storage. Indexing maps an index tuple to a storage offset, fully determined by size, stride and storage_offset.

props.label: 5 doors per row · 1 door per column

cap.1: A card in your pocket says: walk 5 doors for every row down, 1 door for every column across. Row 2, column 3 is door 2×5 + 3 = 13.
cap.2: That card is the stride. x.stride() on a fresh (4, 5) tensor gives (5, 1): skip 5 elements to move one row, 1 to move one column.
cap.3: stride[k] is the number of storage elements skipped per unit step in dim k. A contiguous (4, 5) tensor has strides (5, 1): row-major, last axis fastest.

cap.1: The whole trick is one line. Begin where your view starts, walk 5 doors per row and 1 per column. The exercise is just filling in this card.
cap.2: offset = storage_offset + i·stride[0] + j·stride[1]. Size says how far each index may run; stride says how far each step jumps in memory.
cap.3: In general offset = storage_offset + Σₖ iₖ·strideₖ. Contiguous row-major means each strideₖ is the product of all later sizes; any other pattern is a non-contiguous view.

cap.1: Reshape into 2 rows of 10 and no house moves. You just get a new card: 10 doors per row, 1 per column. Same street, new shape.
cap.2: x.view(2, 10) copies nothing. It returns size (2, 10) and stride (10, 1) over the same storage. Old row 2 (houses 10 to 14) is still one unbroken run.
cap.3: A view shares storage: only size, stride and offset change, so making one is O(1) and in-place writes show up in the original. Cheap, and occasionally surprising.

props.label: 0 doors per row · 1 door per column

cap.1: Now the card says walk 0 doors per row. Every row visits the same five houses. You see four rows, but nothing was copied.
cap.2: Stride 0 is how broadcasting and expand work: a stretched axis never moves in memory, so repeating a row costs nothing at all.
cap.3: A size-n axis with stride 0 aliases one element n times (stride aliasing). expand and broadcasting build exactly this view, so they allocate no new memory.

chapters.name: Read the real card
chapters.verdict: as_strided trusts your card blindly. Read the real one.

cap.1: Transpose rewrites the card and leaves the houses alone. Work out directions from the shape instead of the card and you walk to wrong doors. Nobody stops you.
cap.2: Your as_strided conv passes on fresh inputs, then returns garbage on a transposed or sliced one. Fix: build strides from x.stride(), or call x.contiguous() first.
cap.3: as_strided indexes raw storage from storage_offset with no bounds check. After a transpose or step-2 slice, shape-derived strides describe a layout the tensor no longer has.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: einops patterns compile to size + stride

cap.1: Sliding windows, broadcasting, reshapes: all new cards for the same street. Knowing that makes the layers inside a model feel less like magic.
cap.2: A convolution is a strided window view times a kernel. Broadcasting is stride 0. You will rarely write as_strided yourself, but it explains everything built on top.
cap.3: Linear through Conv2d all rest on views over storage. Knowing view from copy keeps internals legible when you read and edit activations to understand and steer models.

coda.title: Rewrite the directions card and count how often each house gets read
coda.f: range(20).map(h => sum(range(4).map(i => sum(range(n1).map(j => i*s0 + j*s1 === h ? 1 : 0)))))

caption.1: Start at (5, 1): every house read once. Drop row stride to 0 and watch the rows pile onto the same five houses. That pile is broadcasting.
caption.2: Set 1 column and row stride 6: you read houses 0, 6, 12, 18, the diagonal. Then crank the strides until reads run past house 19. Nothing stops you.
caption.3: Each bar counts (i, j) with i·s₀ + j·s₁ = h. Stride 0 aliases; size (4, 1) with s₀ = 6 is the base's diagonal; offsets past numel - 1 are read unchecked.

where_else: Convolution: the sliding window is a strided view of the input, contracted with a kernel
Broadcasting: a stretched axis is just an axis with stride 0
einops: the readable pattern string compiles down to a size and a stride
NumPy arrays carry strides too: the same flat buffer plus a rule

hamming.what: A tensor is one flat run of memory plus a stride per axis saying how far to jump for each index step.
hamming.when: Whenever you transpose, slice, broadcast or build a sliding window, and whenever a view returns numbers that look plausible but wrong.
hamming.why: It lets many shapes share one block of memory for free, which is why transposes and broadcasts cost nothing and why a wrong stride fails silently.

object.title: The street of pillars
object.subtitle: A 4 × 5 window onto one street of 20 houses; each pillar stands as tall as the house number it reads.

cap.1: Each pillar is one slot in your 4 × 5 view. Its height is the house number it reads from the street.
cap.2: Bar height = storage offset of index [i, j] under stride (5, 1).
cap.3: Height encodes i·s₀ + j·s₁ with storage_offset 0; the default is the contiguous row-major layout.

cap.1: With the card (5, 1), heights climb in one smooth run: each row picks up exactly where the last one ended.
cap.2: Contiguous: the last axis moves 1 house at a time, and each row starts 5 houses after the one before.
cap.3: Row-major contiguity: stride₁ = 1 and stride₀ = size₁ = 5, so index order equals memory order.

cap.1: Set row stride to 0. Every row reads the same five houses. Four rows, zero copies.
cap.2: Stride 0 along rows is a broadcast row. This is the view expand builds.
cap.3: A stride-0 axis aliases storage: all four rows point at offsets 0 to 4.

cap.1: Now row stride 1 and column stride 0: each row repeats one house all the way across. A column, stretched sideways.
cap.2: Stride (1, 0) broadcasts a column: row i reads house i five times.
cap.3: Stride (1, 0) is a length-4 vector expanded along dim 1: aliasing along the zero-stride axis.

cap.1: Push the strides too far and the tallest pillars point past house 19. Real code would read garbage and never complain.
cap.2: With stride (6, 2), index [3, 4] reads house 26 of a 20-house buffer. as_strided allows it silently.
cap.3: Max offset Σ(sizeₖ - 1)·strideₖ = 3·6 + 4·2 = 26 exceeds numel - 1 = 19, and as_strided performs no bounds check.

predict.q: You transpose a (4, 5) tensor. How many numbers move in memory?

options.t: None: the stride card flips from (5, 1) to (1, 5)
All 20 get copied into the new order

predict.why: Transpose only permutes strides and leaves memory alone. A copy happens only when you ask for one, for example with .contiguous().

predict.q: An axis has stride 0. What do you see along it?

options.t: The same element repeated, at no memory cost

predict.why: Stride 0 means walk zero doors: every index along that axis reads the same house. That is why broadcasting is free.

predict.q: Your as_strided strides are too big for the buffer. What happens?

options.t: You silently read wrong numbers, even past the end

predict.why: as_strided does no bounds checking. It walks exactly the card you hand it.

object.where: Transposes, broadcasts, sliding windows and einops patterns are all this: one street, a new directions card.
